la:adj:Peducaeus.html:
Pĕdūcaeus, i, m.,
a Roman surname. —So, Sex. Peducaeus, a prœtor in Sicily when Cicero was quœstor there, .—Hence,
Pĕdūcaeā-nus, a, um, adj., Peducœan: ??ensus Peducaeanus,.—
Pĕdūcaeus, a, um, adj., Peducœan: Rogatio Peducaea de incestu, by the people's tribune, Sex. Peducaeus (A. U. C. 640), .

la:noun:pedis.html:
pĕdis, is, comm.
pes
,
a louse: est pedis unus ingens in naso, Nov. ap. : e capite et e collo eorum crebro eligendi pedes,: ubi quamque pedem videbat, Plaut. Vidular. Fragm. : pedes pulicesque, (cited ap. Fest. s. v. pedibus, p. 210 Müll.); Lucil. ap. Fest. l. l.: pulicesne an cimices an pedes, Liv. Andron. ib.

senses: to prop up trees or vines
la:verb:pedo.html:
pĕdo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
pes
,
to foot, i. e. to furnish with feet; hence, *
Male pedatus, ill set on his feet, .—
To prop up trees or vines: vineae pedandae cura,.

la:adv:pedetemptim.html:
pĕdĕtemptim or pĕdĕtentim, adv.
pes-tendo; qs. by stretching out the feet; cf. Doed. Syn. 3, p. 98; hence
,
step by step, slowly (syn.: paulatim, sensim).
Lit.: expectando excrucior. Pa. Pedetemptim, : pedetemptim et sedato nisu, Pac. ap. (Trag. Rel. p. 91 Rib.).—Of elephants: quaerendis pedetentim vadis, in terram evasere,—
Trop., by degrees, gradually, cautiously (class.): sensim et pedetemptim, Lucil. ap. ; cf. : pedetemptim et gradatim accessus,; cf.: paulatim et ut dicitur pedetentim interrogando,: timide et pedetemptim istuc descendunt,; cf.: caute pedetemptimque omnia dicere,: viam tentare, Cato ap. P.: di bene vortant quod agas! pedetemptim tamen,.—Comp.: pedetemptius tibi consulam, M. Aur. ap. .

la:noun:pedes.html:
pĕdes, itis, m.
pes
,
one that is or goes on foot.
In gen.: etiam si pedes incedat,on foot, afoot,: cum pedes iret in hostem,: silvā pedes errat in altā,.—Esp., apposit.: etiam si pedes incedat,: Macedones sciverunt ne (Alexander) pedes venaretur,: ipse equo desiluit, pedesque per nives ingredi coepit,: agmen circumibat pedes,.—
In partic.
A foot-soldier: postulavit ne quem peditem ad colloquium Caesar adduceret,: equitum et peditum copiae, foot-soldiers, foot, Pomp. ap. , C, 1: tria milia et septingenti pedites ierunt,.—
Collect., in sing., foot-soldiers, infantry. cum pedes concurrit, : in pedite robur,: simul pedes, eques, classis apud praedictum amnem convenere,; .—
Transf.: equites pedites, as a general designation for the entire people; cf. colloq. Engl. horse, foot, and dragoons: equitum peditumque prolem describunto,: omnes cives Romani equites peditesque,: Romani tollent equites peditesque cachinnum,.— In sing.: quodvis genus hominum ibi videas, equitem, peditem,.—
A land-soldier (opp. to a marine, classicus): classicae peditumque expeditiones,.

la:adj:pedester.html:
pĕdester, tris, tre (
masc. pedestris, ; ), adj.
id.
, on foot, that goes, is done, etc., on foot, pedestrian.
Lit.: gratior illi videtur statua pedestris futura, quam equestris,: equestres et pedestres copiae,foot-soldiers, infantry,: copiae,; ; so, pedester exercitus,: pedestre scutum,of a foot-soldier,: pugna,: proelium duplex equestre ac pedestre commisit,: pedestris acies,.—
In plur. subst. pedestres, foot-soldiers, ; people on foot, ; .—
Pedestria auspicia nominabantur, quae dabantur a vulpe, lupo, equo, ceterisque animalibus quadrupedibus, Paul. ex Müll.—
Transf., on land, by land: pedestres navalesque pugnae,: pedestria itinera,the roads by land,; cf. : proelia pedestria,: transitus,; . —
Trop., of style, like the Gr. πεζός, not rising above the ground, not elevated.
Written in prose, prose (Gr. idiom; Lat. prosa oratio): Plato multum supra prosam orationem et quam pedestrem Graeci vocant, surgit,: pedestres historiae,.—
Plain, common, without poetic flights, without pathos, prosaic: dolet sermone pedestri Telephus,: quid prius inlustrem satiris musāque pedestri, (for which: sermones Repentes per humum,): opus,: fabulae, P.

la:adj:pedisequus.html:
pĕdĭsĕquus, and lesscorrectly pĕdis-sĕquus, old form pĕdĭsĕcus, a, adj.
pes-sequor
,
that follows on foot: SERVVS PEDISSEQVVS,.—Hence, subst.: pĕdĭsĕquus, i, m., a male attendant; a footman, man-servant, page, lackey; and, pĕdĭsĕqua, ae, f., a female attendant, a waiting-woman, ; ; ; : gnatae pedissequa nutrix anus,; : vestem, uniones, pedisequos et cetera,: clamore pedisequorum nostrorum,; : turba pedisequorum, prooem. 12.—Comically: Pa. Sequere hac me. Py. Pedisecus tibi sum, I'll follow at your heels, immediately, .—
Trop., a follower, attendant: istam juris scientiam eloquentiae tamquam ancillulam pedisequamque adjunxisti,: vix satis idoneae (divitiae) tibi videbuntur, quae virtutis pedisequae sint,the handmaids of virtue,: sapientem quippe pedisequum et imitatorem dei dicimus et sequi arbitramur deum,.

la:adj:pedalis.html:
pĕdālis, e, adj.
pes
,
of or belonging to the foot, foot-.
In gen.; hence, subst.: pĕdālis, is, f. (sc. solea), a slipper, Petr 56.—
In partic., of the size of a foot, of a foot, as a measure; a foot in length, breadth, thickness, etc.: sol mihi videtur quasi pedalis,a foot in diameter,; cf. : transtra ex pedalibus in latitudinem trabibus,: longitudo,: crassitudo,: altitudo,: spatium,: intervalla,: sulcus,.—Subst.: pĕdālis, is, f., a measure; in gen.: tuae praecisionis,.
